introduction: These passages take up evolution in two senses. One is the growth of every being by gradual degrees, as a tree unfolds from its seed and a person from an embryo. The other is the nineteenth-century debate about human origins, in which ‘Abdu’l-Bahá grants that the human form passed through many shapes over immense time while holding that humanity was always a distinct kind, and that development continues in the spirit when the body is complete. Sixty-nine outside voices are set beside them: Genesis, the Psalms, Paul and the Qur’an on formation and stages; an Upanishad, Aristotle and Rumi on the ascent of being; and Darwin, Huxley, Tennyson, Whitman and Nietzsche, who lived through the argument.
questions: The passages compare the history of the species to the growth of an embryo. What does the comparison explain, and where do Darwin's sentences press on it?
Rumi, Emerson and Whitman each tell of an ascent through mineral, plant and animal. How do their versions differ from one another and from these talks?
Genesis speaks of six days, and Peter and the Qur’an of a day as a thousand years. How do these readings treat scripture's account of creation?
Huxley said ethical progress means combating the cosmic process; Tennyson said, move upward, working out the beast. Is spiritual development a continuation of nature or a turn against it?
A later letter leaves questions such as the age of humanity to scientists. How should the statements in this guide be read in the light of that?
One passage says the conditions after death can no more be conceived than the mineral could conceive the plant. What does that argument rest on?

outside.why: Jesus describes the same law of gradual degrees in a seed: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain.
An Upanishad makes the lesson with a fig seed: the great tree exists in an essence too fine to be seen.
Aristotle observed that nature advances by such small steps from the lifeless to the living that no line can be drawn.
A psalm wonders at the same unseen formation in the womb, where a person is already known before being complete.
Darwin concludes that for all his noble qualities man bears in his body the stamp of a lowly origin. Does the embryo comparison in this passage answer him, or describe the same facts differently?
Hamlet lists the wonders of humanity in a single breath and then calls man a quintessence of dust. What would have to be true for the praise to stand without the despair?
A psalm gives humanity the same high station, crowned with glory and set over the works of creation.
Paul uses the same stages of one life to explain how understanding changes while the person remains.
Wordsworth compresses the continuity of one life through its stages into a line: the child is father of the man.
The Qur’an appeals to the same fact in seven words: God created you by stages.
Jaques also counts the ages of a life, and ends them in second childishness and oblivion. What makes the difference between stages that decline and stages that lead upward?
The letter to the Hebrews applies bodily growth to the spirit: milk for infants, solid food for the mature.
This is the passage of the Qur’an that the letter quotes, tracing the body's formation step by step.
Job describes his own making in the same gradual way: poured out, curdled, clothed with skin and knit with bones.
The Preacher admits that the growth of a child in the womb is as hidden from us as the works of God.
Whitman sees himself as the wise man here sees the egg: the summit of what has been and the container of what will be.
Jesus pictures the kingdom of heaven as the smallest seed that becomes a tree where birds lodge.
Tennyson closes his long poem with the same expectation of one distant event toward which the whole creation moves.
The Preacher's lines on a time to plant and a time to pluck up are the old statement that growth cannot be hurried.
The Qur’an says that the human being was created in the best stature.
Genesis sets humanity apart from the first as the one creature made in the image of God.
The Qur’an asks whether there was a time when man was a thing unremembered. How might that question be read beside the claim that the human species existed from the beginning?
Nietzsche tells his hearers that they have come from the worm and were once apes. What is gained and what is lost when human distinctness is denied?
The Preacher in a dark mood says that man has no pre-eminence over a beast, for all are dust. How do these passages answer him?
Genesis also gives living kinds a beginning in time, called out of the earth at a word.
The voice from the whirlwind asks Job where he was when the earth's foundations were laid. How far can rational or spiritual arguments about origins reach?
The Qur’an speaks of the heavens and the earth as once of one piece and then parted, and of every living thing made from water.
Darwin ends his book contemplating a tangled bank of varied forms produced by the same laws.
Darwin too finds grandeur in the thought of endless forms from one or a few beginnings.
Rumi tells the same ascent through mineral, plant and animal to the human, and asks why he should fear the next step.
Emerson's verse has the worm climbing through every form in its striving to be man.
Pope's chain of being is a fixed order in which each link keeps its place. Here the degrees are traversed. What changes when a ladder of being becomes a path?
Genesis has life begin in the waters before it appears on land.
Darwin allowed himself one sentence on the subject in 1859: light will be thrown on the origin of man. How do you read this passage's rejection in the light of what has since been learned?
The Qur’an uses the same image of humanity as a growth raised from the earth.
The Qur’an speaks of the creation of man as something begun from clay, a process with a first stage.
Whitman imagines his own embryo prepared by the whole history of the earth, from nebula to strata to ancient creatures.
Genesis says that man was formed from the dust of the ground, the same earthly elements, and then given breath.
The Preacher finds the same constancy: what has been is what shall be.
Heraclitus holds that everything flows and nothing stays. Five thousand years show no change in the human frame; what would a far longer span show?
A psalm of great age gives the same measure of a human life: seventy years, or eighty.
These are the closing words of the account of creation in days that the talk reads as a symbol.
The second letter of Peter already loosens the days: with the Lord one day is as a thousand years.
The Qur’an says the same of God's reckoning: a day with him is as a thousand years of ours.
Pope places man on an isthmus between beast and angel, the glory, jest and riddle of the world. Is the choice between ape and Divine Spirit a choice between two true descriptions?
A psalm asks what man is that God should be mindful of him, and answers with his dignity.
Nietzsche also sees man as a stage to be passed, a rope toward something higher, but with no will behind the process other than man's own. What does a Primal Will add?
Paul pictures the whole creation labouring together toward something not yet born.
The letter to the Ephesians sets the goal of growth as a perfect humanity, measured by the stature of Christ.
Pope describes one power changed through all things and yet in all the same.
Genesis tells Adam that he is dust and will return to dust. In what sense is man indestructible if his atoms only pass onward?
The letter of James names the same source for every advance: each good gift comes down from above.
Paul reasons from the seed that what is sown must die to be given a new body.
Jesus says that a grain of wheat remains alone unless it dies, and then bears much fruit.
Genesis gives the same permission after the flood: every moving thing that lives shall be food.
Proverbs sets the limit this passage sets: a righteous person has regard for the life of his animal.
Bentham moved the question about animals from reason to suffering. How much weight does this passage's proviso against cruelty carry when human welfare is the purpose?
Paul asks that every task be done heartily, as work for God and not for people.
Herbert's hymn says that work done as for God makes drudgery divine, even the sweeping of a room.
Tennyson turns evolution into a moral call: move upward, working out the beast.
Huxley, Darwin's defender, held that ethical progress means combating the cosmic process, not imitating it. Does this passage treat virtue as a continuation of nature's ascent or as a break with it?
Paul states an order of development: first what is natural, afterwards what is spiritual.
Paul speaks of a natural body and a spiritual body, the second raised when the first is complete.
Heraclitus has a saying for the arc of descent and return: the way up and the way down are one.
Paul says of what is prepared that eye has not seen it nor has it entered the heart.
The first letter of John makes the same admission: it does not yet appear what we shall be.
A psalm measures God's time in a way that leaves room for long ages: a thousand years are as yesterday.
Xenophanes said that the gods did not reveal everything at the start, and that by seeking people find out better in time.
Pope's couplet on a little learning gives the reason for reading the statements together: drink deep, or not at all.

mark-blade-ear-full-corn.text: So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the ground; And should sleep, and rise night and day, and the seed should spring and grow up, he knoweth not how. For the earth bringeth forth fruit of herself; first the blade, then the ear, after that the full corn in the ear

psalm-made-in-secret.text: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well. My substance was not hid from thee, when I was made in secret, and curiously wrought in the lowest parts of the earth. Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them

job-clothed-me-with-skin.text: Remember, I beseech thee, that thou hast made me as the clay; and wilt thou bring me into dust again? Hast thou not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese? Thou hast clothed me with skin and flesh, and hast fenced me with bones and sinews

ecclesiastes-bones-do-grow.text: As thou knowest not what is the way of the spirit, nor how the bones do grow in the womb of her that is with child: even so thou knowest not the works of God who maketh all

ecclesiastes-no-preeminence-above-a-beas.text: For that which befalleth the sons of men befalleth beasts; even one thing befalleth them: as the one dieth, so dieth the other; yea, they have all one breath; so that a man hath no preeminence above a beast: for all is vanity. All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again

And God created great whales, and every living creature that moveth, which the waters brought forth abundantly, after their kind, and every winged fowl after his kind: and God saw that it was good

genesis-let-the-earth-bring-forth.text: And God said, Let the earth bring forth the living creature after his kind, cattle, and creeping thing, and beast of the earth after his kind: and it was so. And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good

genesis-rested-on-the-seventh-day.text: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them. And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made

genesis-every-moving-thing-meat.text: Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you; even as the green herb have I given you all things

psalm-knoweth-our-frame.text: For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust

hebrews-leaving-the-principles.text: For every one that useth milk is unskilful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe. But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil

ephesians-perfect-man.text: Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ

psalm-ninety-yesterday.text: For a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past, and as a watch in the night

quran-growth-from-the-earth.text: And Allah hath caused you to grow as a growth from the earth,

quran-best-stature.text: Surely We created man of the best stature

quran-day-as-thousand-years.text: And they will bid thee hasten on the Doom, and Allah faileth not His promise, but lo! a Day with Allah is as a thousand years of what ye reckon.

quran-began-creation-of-man-from-clay.text: Who made all things good which He created, and He began the creation of man from clay;

quran-product-of-wet-earth.text: Verily We created man from a product of wet earth; Then placed him as a drop (of seed) in a safe lodging; Then fashioned We the drop a clot, then fashioned We the clot a little lump, then fashioned We the little lump bones, then clothed the bones with flesh, and then produced it as another creation. So blessed be Allah, the Best of creators

shakespeare-seven-ages.text: All the world's a stage, / And all the men and women merely players: / They have their exits and their entrances; / And one man in his time plays many parts, / His acts being seven ages

And yet, to me, what is this quintessence of dust

whitman-acme-of-things.text: I am an acme of things accomplish'd, and I an encloser of things to be

emerson-worm-mounts.text: A subtle chain of countless rings / The next unto the farthest brings; / The eye reads omens where it goes, / And speaks all languages the rose; / And, striving to be man, the worm / Mounts through all the spires of form
emerson-worm-mounts.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

nietzsche-rope-over-an-abyss.text: Man is a rope stretched between the animal and the Superman—a rope over an abyss

huxley-combating-the-cosmic-process.text: Let us understand, once for all, that the ethical progress of society depends, not on imitating the cosmic process, still less in running away from it, but in combating it
huxley-combating-the-cosmic-process.author: Thomas Henry Huxley

darwin-light-will-be-thrown.text: In the distant future I see open fields for far more important researches. Psychology will be based on a new foundation, that of the necessary acquirement of each mental power and capacity by gradation. Light will be thrown on the origin of man and his history
darwin-light-will-be-thrown.author: Charles Darwin

whitman-nebula-cohered.text: My embryo has never been torpid, nothing could overlay it. / For it the nebula cohered to an orb, / The long slow strata piled to rest it on, / Vast vegetables gave it sustenance, / Monstrous sauroids transported it in their mouths and deposited it with care
whitman-nebula-cohered.author: Walt Whitman

nietzsche-from-the-worm-to-man.text: Ye have made your way from the worm to man, and much within you is still worm. Once were ye apes, and even yet man is more of an ape than any of the apes
nietzsche-from-the-worm-to-man.author: Friedrich Nietzsche

darwin-lowly-origin.text: man with all his noble qualities, with sympathy which feels for the most debased, with benevolence which extends not only to other men but to the humblest living creature, with his god-like intellect which has penetrated into the movements and constitution of the solar system—with all these exalted powers—Man still bears in his bodily frame the indedible stamp of his lowly origin
darwin-lowly-origin.author: Charles Darwin

psalm-threescore-years-and-ten.text: The days of our years are threescore years and ten; and if by reason of strength they be fourscore years, yet is their strength labour and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away
